title: Backspace String Compare
statement:
The comment box in a feed app records every keystroke so drafts can be synced between devices. A log is a string: a letter means "type this letter", and # means "backspace", which deletes the most recent character still in the box. A backspace on an empty box does nothing.

Two devices sent logs s and t for the same comment. Write def solution(s, t) that returns True if both logs produce the same final text, otherwise False.

The simple answer uses O(n) extra space. Try for O(1) extra space.
constraints: s and t contain only lowercase letters and #

think.q: What does # do, and what if the box is empty?
think.a: It deletes the latest character still in the box. On an empty box it does nothing, so "#a" is just "a". You only compare the final texts; how each device got there does not matter.
"ab##": a, ab, a, empty. "c#d#": c, empty, d, empty. Both end empty, so True.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Replay each log with a stack (a Python list): append letters, pop() on # if the list is not empty, then compare "".join(...). O(n) time and O(n) space. This is a fine first answer to say out loud.

think.q: How do you get O(1) space?
think.a: Two pointers from the end. Reading right to left, a # tells you before you reach a character whether it will be deleted: keep a skip count per string. Move each pointer to its next surviving character and compare them one pair at a time.

1. Helper next_kept(text, i): walk left; on # do skip += 1; on a letter with skip > 0 do skip -= 1; otherwise return i. Return -1 if you fall off the start.
  2. Start i, j at the last kept characters.
  3. While both are valid: if the characters differ, return False; else step both to their next kept characters.
  4. Return True only if both reached -1 together.

More backspaces than letters ("a##c"). Both texts empty. One text is a prefix or suffix of the other ("ab" vs "b"): the loop ends with one pointer still valid. Deletions that span earlier backspaces ("bxj##tw" vs "bxo#j##tw"). Empty logs.

hints: First get it right: build the final text with a list as a stack (append letters, pop on #) and compare.
For O(1) space, read from the right. When you see #, you know the next letter to the left (that is not itself cancelled) will be deleted. Count pending backspaces in skip.
Write a helper that returns the index of the next surviving character to the left (or -1). Compare s[i] and t[j], then move both. At the end both must be -1; if only one is, the lengths differ.
explain:
Example 1, s = "ab#c", t = "ad#c":

  • Last kept characters: s[3] = c, t[3] = c. Equal.
  • Step left in s: index 2 is #, skip = 1; index 1 b is skipped; index 0 a is kept. Same in t: d is skipped, a is kept. Equal.
  • Both helpers return -1 next. Both ran out together, so True.

Why from the end: going left to right you cannot know whether a letter survives until you see the future. Going right to left, every # that could delete a letter has already been seen. Each index is visited once, so it is O(n + m) time with a few integers of space. The stack version is easier to get right in an interview; say it first, then offer this.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space (the stack version is O(n + m) space)

talk: First answer: a list as a stack, append on a letter, pop() on # only if the list is not empty, then compare the joined strings. O(n) time and space.
O(1) space: two pointers from the end with a skip counter per string. A # only affects characters to its left, so reading right to left I always know whether the next letter survives.
I put the skip logic in one helper, next_kept(text, i), so both strings use the same code and the main loop stays three lines.
Termination check: after the loop both indices must be -1. If one string still has a kept character, the texts have different lengths.
Avoid text = text[:-1] in a loop: each slice copies the string, so it is O(n^2) in the worst case. A list with pop() is O(1) per key.
extensions: Add a "delete word" key that removes back to the previous space. How does the right-to-left scan change?
The logs arrive as two live streams. Can you still compare in O(1) space, or do you now need a stack?
Add an undo key that restores the last deleted character. Which approach still works?
Return the final text for one log in O(n) time without a list (hint: write into a list of characters in place, the classic two-pointer compaction).

tests.label: backspace on an empty box
tests.why: extra backspaces do nothing; both become c

tests.label: suffix match only
tests.why: the last characters match but s has one more

perf.label: performance: logs of 120,001 and 60,001 keystrokes whose final texts differ only in the first character
